summary: Defines an extension of the Point-to-Point Protocol for using point-to-point lines for remote bridging of local networks. It is a standards-track document and was replaced by RFC 1638.

plainLanguage.summary: Two office networks far apart can be joined with a phone line so they act like one. This explains how PPP carries that.

questions: what is the ppp bridging control protocol
subtitle: Extending Point-to-Point lines to bridge separate local networks

tldr.problem: Organizations need to connect their office networks across distance using leased lines or dial-up connections, so remote sites can access the same resources as if they were on the same local network.
tldr.mechanism: PPP Bridging allows a point-to-point line to carry entire LAN frames from one site to another, preserving the network layer protocol and MAC addresses. Bridges at each end use standard bridging algorithms (transparent bridging or source routing) across the serial link.
tldr.outcome: Remote bridging enabled geographically dispersed networks to act as one extended LAN. The specification was replaced by RFC 1638, which updated the bridging definitions.

today: RFC 1220 is a Proposed Standard that was replaced by RFC 1638, which updated the PPP bridging specification. Remote bridging over PPP became less common as dedicated WAN protocols and newer technologies emerged, but the techniques remain relevant for certain deployments.

sections.title: Remote Bridging and PPP
sections.content:
This RFC extends PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) to support remote bridging. A bridge is a device that forwards network frames between multiple interfaces based on their destination address, making separate networks appear as one.

In a local network, a bridge learns which addresses live behind which ports by observing source addresses. When a frame is addressed to an unknown destination, the bridge forwards it to all ports except the one it came from (flooding). Standards like IEEE 802.1 define how bridges detect and prevent loops (using spanning tree algorithms).

Remote bridging applies the same principles to a serial point-to-point link. Each end of the link acts as a bridge, forwarding LAN frames across the line while also running bridging algorithms to ensure the extended network remains loop-free.

Two major bridging standards are covered: IEEE 802.1 Transparent Bridging (used for Ethernet and most LANs) and IEEE 802.5 Source Routing (used for Token Ring, where each frame carries its own route).
sections.plainLanguage: A bridge is like a mail sorter that learns addresses. Two remote bridges on each end of a phone line can transfer mail (LAN frames) between the networks, learning which addresses are on which side.

sections.title: Transparent Bridging Across Serial Links
sections.content:
Transparent bridging maintains a forwarding database of addresses observed on each interface. When a frame arrives, the bridge checks if the destination address is in the database. If found, it forwards the frame to the indicated interface. If not found, it floods the frame to all other interfaces.

However, redundant paths in the network can cause frames to loop forever. To prevent this, the Spanning Tree Protocol (IEEE 802.1d) runs between bridges, automatically disabling certain links to form a loop-free tree topology.

The root bridge periodically emits Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs). Each bridge learns its path cost to the root and disables ports with high-cost paths. When topology changes occur (a link fails), the spanning tree is recalculated and blocked ports are re-enabled.

For remote bridging, PPP simply models the serial link as an unspecified interface between half-bridges. Spanning Tree PDUs traverse the line just like regular frames, so the two remote bridges participate in the extended spanning tree as if connected by a real LAN link.
sections.plainLanguage: The bridge learns "Alice is on port 1, Bob is on port 2." When a packet for Alice arrives on port 2, the bridge forwards it to port 1. The spanning tree algorithm prevents loops by disabling backup paths.

sections.title: Source Routing for Token Ring Bridging
sections.content:
IEEE 802.5 Token Ring uses a different approach called Source Routing. The sending station decides the path frames take and includes this path in a Routing Information Field (RIF) in each frame's MAC header.

A bridge examines the RIF to determine if the frame is traveling in the forward or reverse direction along its route. The bridge looks for its ring and bridge identifier in the route list and forwards the frame toward the next segment in the path.

Unlike transparent bridging, source routing requires each device (hosts and bridges) to know its own ring-and-bridge identifier. Discovery is performed by sending explorer frames that accumulate the route as they traverse the network.

For remote bridging over PPP, source routing works similarly: the serial link is modeled as an unspecified interface with a ring number. Frames with RIFs are carried across the link, and both ends participate in route discovery as if they were Token Ring bridges.

The RFC notes that multicast handling (broadcast frames and group addresses) in source routing is complex and deferred to other specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: In Token Ring, each frame carries its own route, like a postcard with "go through bridge A, then bridge B." The bridges check the route and forward accordingly.

sections.title: LAN Frame Transmission and Compression
sections.content:
The RFC defines several traffic services to optimize remote bridging over potentially slow serial links.

LAN Frame Checksum Preservation: IEEE 802.1 requires that an extended LAN maintain the same error probability as a single LAN. To achieve this, the LAN Frame Check Sequence (FCS) calculated by the originating station must be preserved end-to-end. PPP does not corrupt the FCS; it is simply passed through.

LAN Frame Checksum Generation: When a station originates a frame locally (not forwarded), it calculates the FCS. If the station does not support hardware FCS calculation, it tags the frame so receiving stations know to calculate the FCS themselves before delivering it to a LAN.

Tinygram Compression: Small frames on slow links are expensive. Many protocols pad messages to a minimum size by filling with zeros. The RFC defines compression that removes trailing zeros from the LAN data section (but not the MAC header or FCS), then tags the frame. Receivers re-add the zeros to reconstruct the frame.

LAN Identification: The RFC allows tagging frames with a LAN ID to restrict which remote LANs can receive them, effectively creating multiple virtual communities across a single serial link.
sections.plainLanguage: To send LAN frames over a slow phone line efficiently: preserve the original checksum, generate new ones when needed, compress small messages by removing padding, and tag frames so only the right networks receive them.

sections.title: Frame Formats and Bridge Network Control Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC defines frame formats for different LAN types. Each frame is encapsulated in PPP with a bridging protocol identifier (0x0031), and includes flags, MAC type (Ethernet, Token Ring, FDDI, etc.), optional LAN ID, destination and source addresses, and the original LAN data.

Bridge Network Control Protocol (BNCP) is the configuration protocol for establishing bridging on a line. It follows the same structure as PPP's Link Control Protocol (LCP) and uses the same code types: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, etc.

BNCP operates in the network-layer protocol negotiation phase (after LCP completes). Before BNCP opens, no LAN traffic is exchanged. Once BNCP succeeds, both ends are configured to forward frames and the spanning tree protocol (for transparent bridging) or RIF-based routing (for source routing) can begin.

The RFC recommends using Magic Number Loopback Detection and Link-Quality-Monitoring because the spanning tree protocol relies on detecting link failures to recalculate the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: BNCP is a protocol that says "let's both prepare to forward LAN frames on this line." Once both sides agree, they can send LAN packets across the phone line.
